cues.text: A Neglected Childhood

Born in 1550 at Bucchianico in the Abruzzo region, Camillus lost his mother as a child and grew up, by his own later account, almost entirely neglected, the son of an army officer largely absent on campaign.
As a young man he followed his father into military service for Venice and then Naples, developing along the way a consuming addiction to gambling that repeatedly reduced him to poverty.
A Providential Wound
An ulcer on his foot, contracted during his military service, obliged Camillus to seek treatment in 1571 at the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome.
He stayed on afterward as a servant — only to be dismissed for card-playing among the patients.
A Franciscan friar's kindness later moved him to seek admission to the order himself, but his chronic leg wound made him unfit for the physical demands of religious life as then required.
A Turn Toward the Sick

Rather than abandon religious life entirely, Camillus redirected his energy into direct care of the sick, returning to San Giacomo Hospital, where his transformed dedication eventually earned him the position of director.
His confessor, St. Philip Neri , encouraged and supported his path toward ordination, which he received in 1584.
Founding the Ministers of the Sick
With two companions, Camillus founded a new congregation in 1586 explicitly dedicated to nursing — the Ministers of the Sick , popularly called the Camillians.
Its members took the traditional three religious vows plus a distinctive fourth vow, binding them for life to the direct service of the sick, even at personal risk during epidemics.
Care Amid Plague and War
Camillus and his brothers became known for extraordinary courage during plague outbreaks in Rome and Naples, remaining at the bedsides of the contagious when others fled.
In 1595 and 1601, he sent members of his order to tend wounded soldiers on active battlefields in Hungary and Croatia.
This was among the earliest organized efforts at what would later be recognized as military field medicine, work later historians have compared to the origins of the Red Cross.
Legacy
Camillus died at Rome in 1614 after years of declining health borne, by all accounts, with the same patience he had brought to his patients.
Canonized in 1746, he was declared co-patron of the sick and of hospitals by Pope Leo XIII in 1886, along with St. John of God .
Pope Pius XI declared him patron of nurses in 1930 — a former gambler and soldier whose own broken health became the very instrument through which he transformed the care of the sick and dying.
